profile.research_note: [batch narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] CyrusOne was founded in July 2000 by David Ferdman and Larry Bursten, who had previously built companies acquired by IXC Communications. Wikipedia coverage of CyrusOne states the company opened what it described as the largest data center in Texas in Carrollton in 2012, the anchor of the Dallas Fort Worth cluster that this registry row is part of, alongside CyrusOne buildings in nearby Allen, Lewisville, and Collin County. CyrusOne also operates a substantial San Antonio campus and an Austin facility, both long-running Texas markets for the company, though no specific acquisition or opening story for San Antonio or Austin individually was located in available sourcing this session. The company was acquired by ABRY Partners in 2007, purchased by Cincinnati Bell for 525 million dollars in 2010, completed an IPO in 2013, and was taken private again in 2022 when Kohlberg Kravis Roberts and Global Infrastructure Partners acquired it for 15 billion dollars. No building specific address or individual MW figures were located in available sourcing this session.

reading.body:
CyrusOne DFW2 publishes 12 MW of IT capacity across 200,000 square feet in Lewisville, a suburb on the northern edge of the Dallas-Fort Worth metro. At 40 kW per rack, a common AI training density, 12 MW of IT load is roughly 300 racks, enough to run a modest GPU cluster but not a hyperscale training environment. At 10 kW per rack, a more typical mixed-enterprise density, the same power supports around 1,200 racks. The operator does not publish power density targets, so neither figure is their claim.

The certifications qualify this campus to host regulated workloads. PCI DSS qualifies it for payment card data environments. HIPAA qualifies it for protected health information. ISO 27001 certifies the information security management system against an international standard. FISMA qualifies it to support U.S. federal agency workloads. SSAE 16 Type II is an audited controls report that satisfies many enterprise procurement requirements. TIA-942 is a data center infrastructure design standard, with tier level not published here.

Within Texas, this site ranks seventh among the eight facilities on this site for which a megawatt figure is published, out of 133 mapped facilities in the state total. Those eight published facilities sum to 315 MW, and DFW2's 12 MW represents roughly 3.8 percent of that disclosed total. Texas is a significant data center state by count, but most operators there publish no capacity figure, so the 315 MW baseline almost certainly understates the real installed base. DFW2 is a mid-sized, compliance-oriented facility, not a leading indicator of AI scaling capacity in the region.
